content.text: In a message addressed to teachers on this special occasion, AKU President, Dr Sulaiman Shahabuddin, recognised their invaluable contributions and reaffirmed the University's commitment to building the capacity of teachers with the aim of supporting the development of a high-quality education system in Pakistan. "Through its teacher education programmes and professional development initiatives, AKU-IED is actively engaged in preparing and empowering teachers who have the potential to create a substantial positive impact in the lives of their students," he said.

"To further this commitment, we, along with our partners, are training 1,000 education fellows for government schools in Gilgit-Baltistan, with the goal of improving the education system in the region and addressing the shortage of quality school teachers."

In Karachi, a panel discussion was held featuring education: Dr Faisal Bari, Dean, School of Education, Lahore University of Management Sciences; Dr Ghazala Siddiqui, Founder and Principal, Generation's School; and Mr Afaq Ahmed, Lecturer, Government Elementary College for Education and Alumnus, Aga Khan University. The discussion was moderated by Professor Farid Panjwani, Dean at IED, Pakistan.

The panelists focused on the causes and consequences of the teacher shortage, as well as potential solutions to the problem. "A major rethinking is required in terms of educational policy. A commission needs to be formed which should provide policy guidelines for the next five to ten years and its recommendations should be ratified by political stakeholders for continuity of this policy," said Dr Bari.

They also highlighted the importance of quality teachers in ensuring quality education for all children. Pakistan has a shortage of over one million teachers and the shortage of teachers is particularly acute in rural areas and in subjects such as science and mathematics.

"Teachers are at the heart of education recovery. Policymakers in public and private sectors need to address the impending challenges in the education sector through a holistic approach. Investment in developing skilled educational professionals for the digital age and remodeling educational policy viz-a-viz out-of-school children is the need of the hour," said Professor Panjwani.

Dr Siddiqui highlighted that the teacher shortage is a global problem, and Pakistan is no exception. "We need to do more to attract and retain qualified teachers, and to invest in their professional development."

Meanwhile, in Dar es Salaam, the Centre for Continuing Education and Life Long Learning (CELL) through IED, EA held a workshop on Developing Learner Competencies Through Active Learning. The workshop brought together over 65 pre-primary, primary and secondary school teachers, managers and heads of schools, daycare providers and other stakeholders in education.

The workshop's main goal was to help participants better understand active learning and how to promote it in their classrooms. Active learning is one of the main strategies that enables students to engage with the subject matter actively in light of the paradigm shift in Competency-Based Curriculum (CBC) across East Africa. It transforms the conventional classroom model from passive listening to active involvement, encouraging critical thinking, problem-solving abilities, and a deeper comprehension of the subject matter. Research shows that active learning improves academic performance and knowledge retention.

"This workshop is about active learning and how we can use active learning to build competencies. All those labels that are given to quality learning and teaching such as holistic education, student engagement, raising achievements etc. characterize active learning," said Dr Nicholas Wachira, Head of Programmes at IED, EA. "Therefore, this workshop is timely and useful because it serves to move us from not just focusing on the outcome of learning but to focus on the process. If you fix the process the outcome will come automatically."

Participants were first given color-coded sticker notes to share their opinions on what they believe to be the three characteristics of active learning. Following that, participants watched a video analysis on the use of active learning and learned how to incorporate effective active learning strategies into lesson plans. The session was quite interesting, and the way it was conducted itself was a good example of active learning.

Ms Linda Buramu, headteacher from Paragon Academy said, "To learn actively, we need to make sure that teaching enables active learning because active learning is fun and exciting with lots of hands -on activities making the students fully engaged in learning with positive attitude and enthusiasm. Learners share their thoughts, opinions and conclusions about a given topic which leads to high level of engagement, building self-confidence within the learners, increasing their motivation to learn as well as acquiring other skills such as innovation, critical thinking, reflection of real-life aspects, creativity, collaboration, communication, social-interaction and interpersonal skills."
Both events in Karachi and Dar es Salaam concluded with musical performances by students.

content.title: Celebrating World Teachers' Day 2023
content.author: carol.oyola
content.description: World Teachers' Day is a special occasion dedicated to appreciating and recognizing the hard work and dedication of educators worldwide. In celebration of this important day, the Aga Khan University Institute for Educational Development in Pakistan and East Africa held concurrent events to address the theme  'The Teachers We Need for the Education We Want: The Global Imperative to Reverse the Teacher Shortage' .
